Quick Read

Oracle (ORCL) sank 8% Friday to about $101, its lowest close since December 2023, extending a seven-session losing streak and a 69% slide from September's record.

Oracle says its OpenAI buildout is fully funded, yet negative free cash flow, delivery deadlines and OpenAI's payments still threaten the $664 billion backlog.

Microsoft (MSFT) covers its AI capital spending with operating cash flow, while Nvidia (NVDA) Vera Rubin racks at Oracle's Shackelford campus approach handover.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) closed Friday at $101.19, down $9.38, or 8.48%. That was its seventh straight losing session. During the day, the stock reached $100.25, its lowest intraday price since December 2023, and it closed above $100.

24/7 Wall St.

The close was also Oracle's lowest since December 2023, when the stock finished at $100.31. The company now has a market value of $315.48 billion, and the average price target on Wall Street is $236.18. That target means about 133% upside.

That gap comes down to cash. Oracle holds $664 billion in remaining performance obligations and expects at least $90 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue. The market is pricing the stock as if a large share of that backlog may never turn into free cash flow.

Oracle responded minutes after the closing bell. How much that response matters depends on which risks a funding plan can actually remove.

A Slide of Almost 70% From the Record Close

Oracle now trades 69.2% below its record close of $328.33 from September 2025. Measured from that day's intraday high of $345.72, the decline is 70.7%.

The stock fell 19.3% this week from a prior-week close of $125.35. That made it Oracle's worst week since the week that ended in late June, when it dropped 19.4%.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Over the last year, the five biggest AI builders turned just 5 cents of every dollar of profit into free cash. Free cash is the cash left after capital spending. A year earlier, it was 53 cents. The rest is going into data centers. In our view, none of them can afford to slow down in this race. Our cash series looks at why in What If Google Slows Its $160 Billion AI Spend?

That is their bet. This piece is about yours. If you have a few million dollars invested, some of it rides on this race, whether you chose it or not. It can come through Nvidia, through your S&P 500 fund, or through Anthropic shares bought yesterday.

The short answer: don't hide in cash, and don't chase the race. Own companies that turn profit into cash and pay you while you wait. And decide now, while it is still your choice. Don't let the next fall make it for you.

Why Decide Now?

Because several big dates are coming.

The Fed decides on Dec 9. An inflation report comes on Dec 10. Oracle, the most stretched AI buyer, is expected to report in mid-December. Big Tech is expected to set out its 2027 spending plans in late January and early February.

Any one of these can move AI stocks hard in a single day. On Nov 5, two days after the midterm vote, Nvidia lost 9.3%. A plan made before those dates is a plan. A plan made after a 20% fall is a reaction. In our view, once you know what to do, waiting is not caution. It is a choice to stay at risk.

A 9.3% drop in Nvidia in one day makes cash look safe. But your savings can still earn income while you wait. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

What Do People Say Instead?

Here are five things we hear, and our answers.

"I'll keep it in cash until things settle." A 3-month Treasury bill pays 4.34%. Inflation is 3.7%. So after inflation, you are standing still. After taxes, you are falling behind. And markets do not stay settled. The S&P 500 has fallen in 20 of the last 75 years. In our view, cash is the right home for money you will spend in a year or two. It is not the right home for a 10-year plan.

"I'll buy Anthropic and ride AI." Maybe. But we measured seven giant US IPOs. All seven traded below their first-day close within six months. At the low, the median drop was 25%. The median is the middle result. We cover this in Anthropic IPO: Buy Day One Or Wait?

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Dell reports its quarterly results on Tuesday, Nov 24, after the market closes. Last quarter it booked $60.9 billion of AI server orders. It ended the quarter with a $95 billion backlog, meaning orders booked but not yet delivered. In May 2024, the backlog was $3.8 billion.

Can those orders still make money? Dell buys memory chips for these servers, and memory has become dearer. Shares of the memory maker Micron are up 206% in a year.

Dell's stock has fallen 9.3% this week, to $312.54 at Thursday's close. Other AI hardware stocks fell with it. HPE fell 5.8% and Micron 11.3%. Dell is now about 47% below its high.

Report days move Dell's stock a lot. Over its last 12 reports, the median next-day move was 10.6%, up or down. The median is the middle result. Six of those moves were up and six were down. The worst was a 17.9% fall.

Dell sits about 47% below its high, and one report day can move it 10% or more. If you are waiting for a better price to buy, your cash does not have to sit idle. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Is Dell Keeping Less Of Each Sales Dollar?

Dell's sales have grown fast, but its gross margin has slipped. Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of making the products. Sales grew 93% from the quarter to Nov 2024 to the quarter to Jul 2026. Gross profit grew 85%.

Why does the margin slip? An AI server is mostly parts made by other companies. These are Nvidia's chips and the memory that sits beside them. So Dell keeps fewer cents per dollar on AI servers than on the rest of its business.

AI servers are also a growing share of Dell's sales. Dell expects $74.0 billion of AI server sales in fiscal 2027, the year to January 2027. It sold $32.5 billion in the first half. That leaves about $20.7 billion a quarter for the second half. Last quarter it sold $16.4 billion. More AI servers and dearer memory both push the margin down.

So far the market has not minded. Dell's two best report days this year came after quarters in which its gross margin fell. The stock rose 21.9% in February and 32.8% in May.

title: Credo Technology Group vs. Western Digital: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Credo Technology Group vs. Western Digital: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool

ORCL

Trading disclosure

The race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage. You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) for 2027.

Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage. While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure. This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth.

The case for Credo Technology Group

Credo Technology Group specializes in high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions designed for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors. It has established key partnerships with Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems.

The demand for faster semiconductor stocks has significantly boosted its financial performance. In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.6 billion, representing a 165.1% increase over the previous period. This expansion led to a net income of roughly $538.3 million and a net margin of about 33.8%.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, meaning the company carries no debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio is approximately 10.2x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $407.0 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Western Digital

Western Digital designs and supplies essential data-storage solutions for enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers. Its product portfolio includes both hard disk drives and flash-based storage serving a global market across Asia and the Americas. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, with three individual clients accounting for 16%, 15%, and 13% of total net revenue in its latest annual report.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $14.5 billion, representing a 43% increase compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was nearly $10.0 billion, which indicates a net margin of roughly 69.2%. This performance suggests a robust recovery in cloud storage demand, which now accounts for nearly 89% of its net revenue.

title: Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
detail:
Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
Daragh Thomas
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 12:04 PM CST 3 min read
ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) fell more than 6% Friday, but Bernstein argues investors are overlooking what would survive a failed AI expansion: its databases, business software and conventional cloud operations.

Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler estimates those businesses could support a $133 share price even if Oracle's AI data-center revenue disappeared, its hardware became worthless and the company still had to pay the debt incurred to build it.

Oracle traded at $103 Friday morning as chipmakers led another day of selling in AI stocks. That's below the $133 Moerdler thinks it would be worth even after a failed AI expansion.

What Remains After an AI Failure?

Bernstein expects Oracle's databases, business software and conventional cloud services to keep earning money even if its AI data-center business fails. Its calculation values those surviving businesses at roughly 25 times their expected earnings over the next year.

In that scenario, Oracle would still have to pay for data centers its AI customers no longer use, and Moerdler says investors may already assume Oracle cannot find replacement tenants, leaving it "holding the proverbial bag" on about $288 billion in lease commitments.

But he thinks Oracle could find other cloud customers to fill those facilities. The payments also stretch over leases lasting as long as 19 years, spreading the bill rather than making it payable all at once.

That argument depends on demand surviving elsewhere. His $133 estimate does not cover a worldwide collapse in generative AI demand, which could make finding replacement customers much harder.

Shares Fall Below the Offering Price

Oracle priced $10 billion of new shares at $116 on Nov. 2, alongside $10 billion of bonds carrying interest rates of 7% to 8.65%.

Friday's price leaves those shares almost 11% below the offering price.

Traders Price a Broader Downturn

On Polymarket, traders put the chance of an AI industry downturn, as the contract defines it, at approximately 26% by June 30th, 2027, with $198,000 traded.

The contract requires three of six triggers in the same 90-day period, including steep stock-price declines and falling computing rental prices. It measures financial stress across the industry, rather than the complete global AI failure Bernstein excludes.

Moerdler remains bullish, with an Outperform rating, equivalent to a buy, and a $325 price target, more than three times Friday's share price.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) fell 2.92% to $110.57 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 19, leaving the database and cloud giant down more than 40% this year. The shares now trade below a severe downside case that Bernstein's Mark Moerdler sketched in a November 18 note.

ORCL GF Value chart

Bernstein kept its Outperform rating and $325 target. Its stress scenario, in which Oracle's AI data-center business failed, the hardware became unusable and Oracle kept the debt, works out to about $133 a share. The balance sheet explains the fear. Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capex last quarter, posted negative free cash flow of $5.4 billion and saw interest expense rise 55% to $1.4 billion, 24/7 Wall St. reported in its review. It expects to raise about $40 billion this fiscal year. Against that, remaining performance obligations total $664 billion, and fiscal 2027 guidance calls for at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS.

The close is about 17% below Bernstein's stress price. On guided EPS, Oracle trades at about 13.7 times earnings. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 88/100, a high-quality grade. GF Value is $201.78, a 45.2% discount, but GuruFocus itself labels Oracle a possible value trap. That warning fits a company whose backlog is huge but funded with borrowed money. The December 14 earnings report is the next test of whether backlog is converting into cash.
